evidence_quotes.quote: is reported by 59% of households in NN slums as against 51% in notified slums.
Dependent variable: local councilor is aware of the water supply condition of slums (AWARE)
Determinants of willingness to opt for privatization (PRIVATE) and pay water charges (CHARGE).

printed_headline_estimate: Out-of-scope logit estimates only: Table 5 (PDF p. 12, survey N = 541), NN -> AWARE (perceived councilor awareness) logit coef = -2.14*** (printed as 2.14*** with negative sign stated in text p. 12; stat in parentheses = 4.63, p < 0.01); Table 7 (PDF p. 15, N = 513), NN -> PRIVATE (Model II willingness to opt for privatization) logit coef = -1.87*** (printed as 1.87*** with negative sign stated in text p. 15; stat = 9.07, p < 0.01), GL -> PRIVATE (Model I) = 2.54*** (7.49, p < 0.01), RL -> PRIVATE (Model I) = -4.06*** (printed as 4.06*** with negative sign in text; 13.54, p < 0.01), NN -> CHARGE (willingness to pay public water charges) = 0.97** (4.41, p < 0.05). Actual water access contrasts (e.g., 59% insufficient water in NN vs. 51% in notified slums, PDF p. 8) report descriptive percentages only without SE/CI/test/p-value.
publication_year_note: Primary journal volume/issue year is 2016 ('Water Policy 18 (2016) 750–768', '© IWA Publishing 2016' on PDF p. 1); online-first publication date is 25 November 2015 ('Available online 25 November 2015' on PDF p. 19, alongside DOI 10.2166/wp.2015.127).
rationale: The full text reports inferential logistic regression models in Table 5 (PDF p. 12) and Table 7 (PDF p. 15), which include legal slum tenure predictors (non-notified slum dummy NN, government land GL, railway land RL). However, none of the inferential models test a Criterion 4 household or community water/sanitation service access outcome: Table 5 tests perceived councilor awareness of slum water conditions (AWARE), and Table 7 tests stated willingness to opt for hypothetical privatization (PRIVATE) or willingness to pay public water charges (CHARGE), where existing water sufficiency (SUFFICIENT) and perceived quality (GOOD_QUALITY) enter only as right-hand-side covariates. All empirical comparisons of actual water supply sufficiency, source distance, water quality, toilet use, and drainage across notified versus non-notified slums or ethnic groups (Section 7, Table 4, PDF pp. 8–10) are purely descriptive percentages with no inferential hypothesis tests, standard errors, confidence intervals, or p-values.
